newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Motor racing-The king of F1 looks to the stock markets.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Motor racing-The king of F1 looks to the stock markets.

text.p: Bernie Ecclestone, the man who revolutionised Formula One motor racing, will never settle for second best.
He has built F1 from a rich man's sport run on semi-Corinthian lines to a multi-million dollar global business.
But the urge to be a winner still burns strongly in Ecclestone.

The head of the Formula One Constructors' Association (FOCA), vice-president for commercial affairs for the International Motoring Federation (FIA) and commercial rights-holder for the FIA's Formula One world championship is now considering a stock market flotation that is likely to make him a billionaire.
Ecclestone is already a multi-millionaire and one of the richest men in Britain, where he lives in a mansion block in Chelsea, London. The nine-storey headquarters also house his offices.
The son of a trawler captain, Ecclestone first became a car dealer and then a motor cycle dealer in which he excelled and made his first major fortune.
He raced himself with limited success. Then he realised he would do better at owning and running teams. In 1958 he bought the Connaught team and 12 years later bought Brabham.
With Brabham he won two world championships. He achieved it with a ruthless will to win and an extraordinary attention to detail.

Dozens of stories are swapped about Ecclestone's strict regime during his time in charge of the team, including one that he threatened to close down the factory if it was not kept tidier than he found it.

To this day such stories are given foundation by Ecclestone's high standards demanded in and around the F1 paddock. He is known to have inspected the toilets at some circuits to ensure they were clean and stocked with toilet paper.
During his time with Brabham he became involved in F1 politics and threw himself into the struggle for power between the teams and the ruling body, the FIA.
He turned FOCA into his power base and used it to take control of events. He began to shape the future direction of the sport and made himself an almost irreplaceable figure in its administration.

Ecclestone emerged as the man to control the calendar, by negotiating all the deals with the promoters, and the television contracts. He also took over control of on-site advertising and various other promotional activity, creating a package which produced huge revenue for the teams.
FIA president Max Mosley said recently: "Between 1969 and today a series like sports car racing has lived and died several times and they have never really come to nothing.
"The reason the overall business of Formula One has worked so well in the same period is down to Bernie. In his way, he is a genius."

Asked to explain why there appeared to be so much envy of Ecclestone's wealth -- generated by his companies' success on behalf of the FOCA and the FIA -- Mosley said: "If somebody makes an extraordinary success of an enterprise, it is not suprising that extraordinary wealth can accompany it.

"Some of the team owners were worried about who would run things if Bernie retired...He is a brilliant negotiator, the best person I have seen at getting the maximum possible price for something and his business brain is astounding."
Ecclestone has, in simple terms, managed to 'grow' Formula One until it became big enough and popular enough to make a success of his massive digital television venture.

"He invested $340 million in that when everone else was saying it would never get off the ground and it is showing every sign of being a great success. That is because he took a huge risk and the teams will benefit from that, too," said Mosley.

Though he can be tough and uncompromising, Ecclestone is also popular in the Formula One paddock with those who are used to him. He trades jokes with reporters, chats with team members and eats in the motor homes.
He shrugged aside criticism he has received for achieving Formula One's growth at the expense, in Melbourne, of causing damage to the environment of Albert Park.
"I don't give a damn what people think of me," he said. "To be honest, I am just doing a job in the best way I can. So maybe I upset a few people along the way."

Tough he may be, but Ecclestone's humour shines through. When, despite organised protesters, Albert Park was transformed in 1996 into a race circuit Ecclestone sent the head of the Australian Grand Prix organisers, Judith Griggs, a thank-you gift.
It was a solid-silver 25-cm tall cement mixer with an inscription: "To Judy, earth mover of the year".
